name: Asparagus
timing: Mid-April through mid-June; peak the last two weeks of May. Spears grow 1–2 inches per day in warm weather — harvest before tips open.
description: One of spring's first arrivals — tender shoots push through cold midwest soil as temperatures rise. Michigan is the nation's top asparagus producer.
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins K and C

name: Rhubarb
timing: Early April through June; harvest stalks before the plant sends up a flower stalk. Do not harvest in the first year after planting.
description: Brilliant crimson stalks with intense tartness. A midwest spring staple for jams, compotes, and pies. Often the first garden harvest of the year.

name: Watercress
timing: April through early June; best before temperatures exceed 70°F, which causes bitterness and bolting. Found wild along cold, clear streams.
description: Peppery aquatic greens found along clear cold streams. Harvested wild or cultivated in spring before summer heat turns them bitter.
nutritionHighlights: Rich in vitamins A, C, and K

name: Green Onions
timing: April through October; available at farmers markets from first thaw. Spring bunches are mildest; summer ones grow stronger-flavored.
description: Slender, mild alliums available through most of the growing season. Indispensable across all three major East Asian cuisines.

name: Spinach
timing: April–June (spring crop, sweet and mild); September–November (fall crop, even better after light frost). Bolts and turns bitter when temperatures exceed 75°F.
description: Tender leaves thrive in cool spring and fall weather. Fall spinach is notably sweeter. Loses flavor quickly in summer heat.
asianUses: Ohitashi (Japanese blanched salad with dashi and soy)
Stir-fried with garlic and sesame oil
nutritionHighlights: High in vitamins A and K

name: Radishes
timing: April–June (spring; 25–30 days from seed to harvest). September–October (fall; slower growth, milder flavor). Some farms grow large Korean/daikon-type radishes in fall.
description: Spring varieties are crisp and peppery; fall radishes grow larger and sweeter. Midwest farms grow both red table radishes and large Asian-type varieties.

name: Garlic Scapes
timing: Late May through June; the curling green flower stalks of hardneck garlic. Cut them off — it improves bulb development and they're delicious. Available for only 2–3 weeks.
description: The tender spiral shoots that grow atop hardneck garlic before bulb harvest. Mildly garlicky with a grassy freshness — one of the most sought-after early summer market items.

name: Shiso (Perilla)
timing: June through September; start indoors in May, transplant after last frost. Leaves are most flavorful before the plant flowers in late August. Pinch blooms to extend harvest.
description: Aromatic Japanese herb in the mint family with a distinctive anise-basil-mint flavor. Grows readily in midwest gardens through summer. Green (aojiso) and red (akajiso) varieties are both useful.
asianUses: Kkaennip (Korean perilla) wraps for grilled meat

name: Peas
timing: May through early July; pick snap peas before the seeds swell visibly in the pod. Sugar peas in the last week of June through July tend to be sweetest. Season ends abruptly when temperatures hit 85°F.
description: Sweet snap peas and shell peas peak in early summer before heat makes pods tough. Particularly delicious eaten fresh from the pod at the farm.
asianUses: Snow peas in stir-fry with shrimp
Chilled pea salad with sesame dressing
nutritionHighlights: High in protein for a vegetable
Rich in vitamins C and K

name: Bok Choy
timing: May–June (spring; bolt risk increases after mid-June); September–November (fall; best after overnight temperatures drop below 60°F). Baby bok choy matures in 30 days.
description: Tender Chinese cabbage that thrives in cool midwest springs and falls. Baby bok choy is especially prized for sweetness and tenderness.
nutritionHighlights: Rich in vitamins A and C

name: Kohlrabi
timing: May–June (spring; harvest when bulb reaches golf-ball to tennis-ball size, about 45–50 days). September–October (fall; flavor improves slightly after light frost).
description: A crisp, mild-flavored bulb that tastes like a cross between broccoli stem and apple. One of the most underutilized midwest vegetables. Both the bulb and the leaves are edible.
asianUses: Chinese stir-fried julienned kohlrabi with garlic
nutritionHighlights: Good source of potassium and fiber

name: Strawberries
timing: First week of June through mid-July; peak quality is the last 10 days of June. Everbearing varieties extend into July. U-pick farms typically open the first weekend of June.
description: Intensely fragrant and sweet, midwest strawberries peak in early June and are far superior to off-season imports. Their season is brief — the flavor deteriorates within days of picking.

name: Sweet Cherries
timing: Second week of July, lasting just 2–3 weeks. Michigan's northwestern orchards peak around July 10–25. Bing and Rainier are the most common varieties — Rainier's yellow-blush skin indicates full ripeness.
description: Dark, juicy sweet cherries ripen in mid-July across Michigan orchards. A brief, precious season — best eaten within days of picking.

name: Tart Cherries
timing: Mid-July through early August; Michigan's Traverse City region harvests Montmorency tarts around July 10–20. The season lasts just 2–3 weeks per orchard.
description: Michigan is the nation's top producer of Montmorency tart cherries. These brilliant red, intensely flavored cherries are ideal for preserves, pies, and juice.
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins A and C

name: Blueberries
timing: Early July through mid-August; southwestern Michigan (Van Buren County) is one of the top producing regions. Northern Michigan farms peak in late July. U-pick typically available for 5–6 weeks.
description: Plump, dusty-blue berries cluster on low bushes across the upper midwest. Michigan ranks among the top producing states in the nation.
nutritionHighlights: Highest antioxidant content of any common fruit
Rich in vitamins C and K

name: Raspberries
timing: Mid-July through August (summer-bearing crop); September (fall-bearing second crop on everbearing varieties). Berries last only 2–3 days after picking.
description: Delicate ruby-red raspberries require careful picking but reward with intense flavor. Some farms have a fall second crop in September.
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins C and K

name: Plums
timing: Japanese-type plums (Burbank, Santa Rosa): late July–August. European prune plums (Italian, Damson): August–September. All ripen over several weeks depending on variety.
description: Juicy stone fruit with a tart skin and sweet flesh. Both Japanese and European varieties grow in midwest orchards, offering a long combined season from July through September.
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamin C and K

name: Cantaloupe
timing: Mid-July through September; peak in August when sugar content is highest. A ripe cantaloupe slips easily from the vine and has a pronounced floral aroma at the stem end.
description: Sweet, fragrant muskmelons grown across the midwest, with heavy production in Illinois and Indiana. The best ones smell like perfume through a paper bag.
nutritionHighlights: High in vitamin C and potassium

name: Watermelon
timing: Mid-July through September; peak in the first two weeks of August. Look for a creamy yellow field spot on the underside — pale or white means unripe. Sugar Baby and icebox varieties ripen 2 weeks before large slicers.
description: Juicy, sweet melons grown across the midwest, especially in Indiana and Illinois. Summer heat is essential for developing the high sugar content midwest watermelons are known for.
asianUses: Watermelon juice (popular in Chinese summer cooking)
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins A and C

name: Peaches
timing: Late July (earliest varieties like Reliance) through September; Michigan peak is the second and third week of August. Best eaten the same day — refrigeration kills the flavor.
description: Fragrant, dripping-ripe midwest peaches are a fleeting late-summer treasure. Michigan's southwestern counties produce some of the finest peaches in the country.
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins C and A

name: Zucchini
timing: Late June through September; best when 4–6 inches long, before July heat makes them watery and seedy. Check plants every 2 days — they grow from perfect to overgrown overnight.
description: Prolific summer squash available in abundance through late summer. Young tender squash is best; overgrown ones become watery and seedy.

name: Thai Basil
timing: June through September; most productive July–August in midwest heat. Pinch flower clusters as they appear to prolong leaf production. Frost kills plants immediately.
description: Aromatic herb with anise-clove flavor essential to Southeast Asian and Taiwanese cooking. Thrives in midwest summer heat. Distinctly different flavor from Italian sweet basil.
asianUses: Three-cup chicken (三杯雞) — added at the last second

name: Cucumbers
timing: Mid-July through September; Japanese thin-skin varieties (Tasty Jade, Summer Dance) ready by early July in warm years. Pick before yellow color appears at stem end.
description: Cool and crisp, cucumbers peak in midsummer. Japanese and Korean thin-skin varieties grow well in midwest gardens and are especially prized for pickling and fresh eating.

name: Cherry Tomatoes
timing: Mid-July through October frost — the first tomatoes to ripen and the last to be killed by cold. A full 4-month season. Sungold, Sweet 100, and Black Cherry are common midwest varieties.
description: Small, intensely sweet tomatoes that ripen weeks before large-fruited types. Cherry tomatoes stay productive all summer and into fall, making them the most reliable fresh tomato.
asianUses: Chinese cherry tomato stir-fry with egg
Korean tomato banchan with sesame oil
nutritionHighlights: Very high in vitamin C relative to size

name: Heirloom Tomatoes
timing: Late July (first heat-set fruits) through September; peak quality the third and fourth weeks of August. Brandywine, Cherokee Purple, and Green Zebra are popular midwest varieties. Crack quickly after heavy rain.
description: Open-pollinated varieties with extraordinary flavor complexity. Heirlooms trade yield and disease resistance for taste — colors range from deep purple to striped green to bright yellow.
asianUses: Japanese heirloom tomato salad with ponzu and shiso
Chinese egg and tomato stir-fry (best with large beefsteak type)
Sliced with soy sauce and sesame oil
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins C and K

name: Roma / Paste Tomatoes
timing: August through October frost; less prone to cracking than slicing tomatoes. San Marzano and Amish Paste varieties are preferred. Best for sauce after the second week of August when sugars are highest.
description: Thick-walled, low-moisture paste tomatoes ideal for sauce, canning, and sundrying. More forgiving than heirlooms — resist cracking after rain and produce a heavy crop.
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins C and K

name: Eggplant
timing: Mid-July through September; Japanese and Chinese slim varieties (Ichiban, Orient Express) ripen a week or two before globe types. Pick when skin is shiny — dull skin means seeds are maturing and flesh is bitter.
description: Slim Japanese and Chinese varieties (lavender-purple, finger-length) thrive in midwest summer heat. Sweeter and less bitter than large globe eggplant.

name: Sweet Corn
timing: Mid-July through September; Illinois and Indiana sweet corn peaks in early August. Sugars convert to starch within 24 hours of picking — shop local and cook immediately. The 'silk test': brown and slightly sticky means ready.
description: The quintessential midwest crop. Roadside stands selling just-picked corn are a summer institution. Local just-picked ears are incomparably sweet.
asianUses: Yaki tōmorokoshi (grilled corn brushed with soy butter)
nutritionHighlights: Contains lutein and zeaxanthin for eye health

name: Green Beans
timing: Mid-July through September; pick before the seeds bulge visibly in the pod. Long (yard-long/asparagus) beans ripen slightly later and prefer hot weather — peak late July through August.
description: Crisp, snappy beans available throughout summer. Long (yard-long) beans also grow well in midwest gardens and are preferred for Asian preparations.
asianUses: Dry-fried Sichuan string beans (干煸豆角)
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins C and K

name: Garlic
timing: Cured bulbs: July–August, after the tops fall over and dry. Freshly harvested 'green garlic' in June-July has milder, sweeter flavor than cured. Hardneck varieties offer more complex flavor than softneck.
description: Fresh-harvested garlic in summer has a sweeter, more complex flavor than cured storage garlic. Hardneck varieties (Rocambole, Porcelain) are preferred by chefs for their nuanced heat.

name: Peppers
timing: Mid-July (green bell peppers); late August–September (red/orange/yellow bells — left on the vine 2–3 more weeks). Hot peppers peak August–October. Korean varieties need full summer heat to develop maximum heat.
description: Sweet bells and hot chili varieties ripen through late summer into fall. Korean varieties (cheongyang, gochugaru types) grow well in midwest heat.
nutritionHighlights: Extremely high in vitamin C (red > green)

name: Edamame
timing: August through October; fresh edamame requires 75–85 days from planting (plant mid-May in midwest). The harvest window per plant is just 5–7 days — pods must be picked when bright green and firm.
description: Fresh soybeans in the fuzzy green pod, grown throughout midwest farm country. The flavor difference between fresh and frozen edamame is dramatic — fresh is sweet and grassy.
asianUses: Boiled with sea salt (classic izakaya appetizer)

name: Shishito Peppers
timing: August through October; pick when 3–4 inches long and still green. The famous 'one in ten is spicy' ratio increases as fall weather cools — harvest before frost.
description: Thin-skinned, mildly hot Japanese peppers that blister beautifully in a dry cast iron pan. About one in ten is surprisingly spicy — part of the Russian roulette appeal.
asianUses: Blistered with flaky salt and lemon (izakaya classic)
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins A and C

name: Beets
timing: Early summer beets (June–July): 50-day varieties, golf ball to tennis ball size. Fall storage beets (September–November): larger, sweeter after light frost. Chioggia (candy-striped) and Golden varieties also available.
description: Earthy and sweet, beets are harvested from early summer through fall. The greens are also edible — don't throw them away. Yellow and chioggia varieties each have distinct, milder flavors.
nutritionHighlights: Rich in nitrates for blood pressure

name: Tomatillos
timing: August through October frost; ripe when the papery husk splits open and the fruit fills it completely. They grow in pairs — two plants minimum for good pollination and yield.
description: Tart, citrusy fruits in papery husks. A warm-season crop that thrives in midwest summer heat. Grown at many midwest farms, especially those serving Latin communities.

name: Fennel
timing: June (spring-planted bulbing fennel) and September–October (fall-planted, best flavor after cool nights). Harvest before plants bolt. Fronds, seeds, and bulb are all useful.
description: Anise-flavored vegetable with a crisp white bulb and feathery green fronds. Less common at midwest markets but available at farms catering to diverse clientele.
asianUses: Chinese fennel and pork dumplings (茴香猪肉饺子)
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamin C and fiber

name: Napa Cabbage
timing: September through November; plant in late July for harvest after first light frost (typically mid-October in midwest). Frost improves sweetness. Full heads need 70–80 days from transplant.
description: The essential kimchi ingredient — grows abundantly in cool fall weather. Heads become sweet and crisp after light frosts. A pillar of Korean autumn food culture.
nutritionHighlights: Rich in vitamins C and K

name: Daikon
timing: September through November; plant in mid-August for October–November harvest. Grows to 12–18 inches long in midwest fall soil. Flavor sweetens after light frost. Smaller Korean kkakdugi-type varieties also available.
description: Large white radishes with mild sweetness and crunch. A cornerstone of Japanese and Korean cooking. Grows to impressive size in cool midwest fall soil.

name: Kabocha Squash
timing: September through November; cure for 2–4 weeks after harvest at room temperature — this converts starches to sugars and dramatically improves flavor. Look for a dry, corky stem.
description: Japanese pumpkin with dense, sweet, chestnut-flavored flesh and a dry texture. Dark green skin, vibrantly orange inside. Grows well in midwest gardens.
nutritionHighlights: Rich in vitamins A and C

name: Butternut Squash
timing: September through November; cure for 4–6 weeks after harvest for best flavor and shelf life. Stores for 3–6 months in a cool, dry location. Flavor continues to develop in storage.
description: Nutty, sweet winter squash with tan skin and bright orange flesh. A prolific midwest fall crop that stores well through winter.
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins C and E

name: Sweet Potatoes
timing: Harvested in October before the first hard frost. Cure for 1–2 weeks at room temperature — this converts starches to sugars and heals the skin. Flavor is mediocre uncured; dramatically better after curing.
description: Orange-fleshed roots grown throughout the midwest, especially in Illinois. Require a long warm season — slip planting in May, harvest 90–120 days later.
asianUses: Satsumaimo (Japanese sweet potato) roasted over stones
Glass noodles (made from sweet potato starch)
nutritionHighlights: Rich in vitamins A and C

name: Leeks
timing: May–June (spring-planted, harvested young and slender); October–November (fall/winter leeks, larger and sweeter after frost). Winter varieties can survive in the ground under mulch in mild midwest winters.
description: Mild, sweet alliums with a long white shaft and dark green tops. More delicate than onions. Grow well in midwest conditions and improve with cool fall weather.

name: Asian Pears
timing: September through November; unlike European pears, Asian pears are ripe when still firm. Test by gentle hand pressure — slight give means perfect. Available at select midwest orchards and Asian markets.
description: Crisp, apple-shaped pears with delicate floral sweetness. Unlike European pears, they are ripe when still firm. Grown in select midwest orchards.
asianUses: Bulgogi and galbi marinade (enzymes tenderize meat)
Japanese pear salad with ginger dressing

name: European Pears
timing: Bartlett: mid-August (earliest, softest). Bosc: September–October (firm, spicy). Anjou: October–November (last). Unlike Asian pears, they're picked firm and ripen off the tree at room temperature over 5–7 days.
description: Classic European pears ripen off the tree, sweetening as they soften. Bartlett, Bosc, and Anjou varieties are all grown in midwest orchards. U-pick pear farms are less common than apples.

name: Apples — Early Season
timing: Lodi and Yellow Transparent: mid-July (soft, best for sauce). Paula Red: late July through mid-August (great fresh-eating, first red apple of the season). Zestar and Gala: late August (crisp and sweet). Earliest varieties have short shelf life — eat within days.
description: The first apples of the season arrive in July and August. Varieties like Paula Red and Zestar are crisp, sweet, and a welcome sign of the upcoming fall harvest.

name: Apples — Honeycrisp & Midseason
timing: McIntosh: early September (soft, best for cider). Cortland: September–October (white non-browning flesh, ideal for salads). Honeycrisp: mid-September through October (the premium pick-your-own variety — expect lines at U-pick farms). Jonathan: September.
description: The peak of apple season. Honeycrisp's legendary crunch and balanced sweetness made it a phenomenon — it was developed at the University of Minnesota and thrives in midwest conditions.

name: Apples — Late Season
timing: Empire: October (McIntosh × Red Delicious cross, stays firm longer). Jonagold: October (very large, sweet-tart). Fuji: October–November (very sweet, slow ripening — Japanese origin, now widely grown in midwest). Braeburn: late October.
description: The final apple varieties of the season bring deep flavor and excellent storage qualities. Late-season apples like Fuji and Empire can be cellared through winter.

name: Grapes
timing: Concord: third week of September (when the distinctive aroma fills the air). Niagara (white Concord): September. Wine varieties: September–October. Concord season is brief — just 2–3 weeks.
description: Concord, Niagara, and wine grape varieties ripen across midwest vineyards in September. The Concord grape's distinctive 'foxy' aroma is uniquely American.
nutritionHighlights: Good source of vitamins C and K

name: Wild Mushrooms
timing: Morels: first two weeks of May (after soil reaches 50°F — usually April 20–May 10 in the central midwest). Chanterelles: late July–August. Hen-of-the-woods (maitake): October. Oyster mushrooms: spring and fall after rain.
description: The midwest's deciduous forests yield exceptional wild mushroom harvests. Morel hunting is a beloved spring tradition; fall brings maitake, chanterelles, and oyster mushrooms.

name: Kale
timing: September through January; flavor improves dramatically after the first hard frost (usually mid-October in the midwest) — cold converts starches to sugars. Lacinato (dinosaur kale) is especially cold-hardy. Can be harvested under snow.
description: Cold-hardy kale is one of the few vegetables available into midwest winter. Frost-sweetened October and November kale is far better than summer kale.
nutritionHighlights: Extremely high in vitamins K and A

name: Gai Lan
timing: April–June (spring; harvest before flower buds open, 60–70 days); September–October (fall; sweeter after overnight lows dip below 55°F). Pick stems before yellow flowers fully open.
description: Chinese broccoli (芥蘭) with glossy leaves and thick stems. A pillar of Cantonese cooking with a pleasantly bitter flavor, deeper than regular broccoli. Widely available at Asian grocery stores.
asianUses: Steamed with oyster sauce (classic Cantonese preparation)
Lo mein and chow fun addition
nutritionHighlights: Very high in vitamins C and K

name: Yu Choy
timing: April–June (spring; matures in 35–40 days, one of the fastest crops); September–October (fall). Harvest when flower buds are just forming — plants become fibrous once in full flower.
description: Tender Chinese flowering greens (油菜心) with small yellow flowers and smooth stems. One of the most popular vegetables in Cantonese cooking — mild, slightly sweet, with delicate texture.
nutritionHighlights: High in vitamins C and K

name: Bitter Melon
timing: July through September; harvest when 4–6 inches long and pale green. Flavor intensifies as it yellows — most Chinese cooks prefer it green. Available at Asian grocery stores.
description: Intensely bitter, distinctively wrinkled green gourd (苦瓜) essential to Chinese, Korean, and Southeast Asian cooking. Grows well in midwest summer heat. An acquired taste with devoted fans.
asianUses: Bitter melon stir-fry with black bean sauce (豉汁苦瓜)
Bitter melon with eggs (苦瓜炒蛋)

name: Garlic Chives
timing: May through October; flat-leaved Chinese chives can be cut several times per season. Flower stalks (韭花) appear in late summer — highly prized. More cold-tolerant than basil.
description: Flat-leaved Chinese chives (韭菜) with a garlic-onion flavor more assertive than Western chives. A cornerstone of Chinese and Korean cooking. The flower buds in late summer are a seasonal delicacy.
asianUses: Garlic chive stir-fry with egg (韭菜炒蛋)
nutritionHighlights: Rich in vitamins A and C

name: Water Spinach
timing: July through September; thrives in midwest summer heat and humidity. Grows semi-aquatically or in very moist soil. Available at Chinese and Southeast Asian grocery stores.
description: Hollow-stemmed aquatic greens (空心菜) essential to Chinese, Thai, and Filipino cooking. The distinctive hollow stems give a unique tender-crisp texture when stir-fried at high heat.
asianUses: Stir-fried with fermented tofu and chili (腐乳炒空心菜)
Thai morning glory stir-fry (pak bung fai daeng)
nutritionHighlights: Rich in vitamins A and C

name: Chrysanthemum Greens
timing: April–June and September–October; cool-season crop that bolts quickly in summer heat. The edible chrysanthemum (not ornamental). Available at Asian grocers.
description: Fragrant, slightly bitter greens (茼蒿) with a distinctive herby-floral flavor. Related to the ornamental chrysanthemum but bred for culinary use. A classic hot pot and nabe vegetable.
nutritionHighlights: Rich in vitamins A and C

name: Chinese Mustard Greens
timing: April–June (spring) and September–October (fall); pungency varies by variety — leaf mustard is milder, stem mustard sharper. Flavor intensifies after light frost.
description: Pungent, peppery greens (芥菜) with broad leaves and thick stems. A staple of Cantonese and Sichuan cooking. Both fresh and pickled forms are widely important in Chinese cuisine.
asianUses: Stir-fried with ginger and oyster sauce
nutritionHighlights: Excellent source of vitamins C and K

name: Luffa
timing: July through September; harvest when 6–10 inches long and still tender. Left to fully mature it becomes the fibrous loofah sponge — but picked young, the flesh is silky and mild.
description: Tender Asian gourd (丝瓜) with mild, slightly sweet flavor and silky texture. Completely different from the mature dried loofah sponge. A beloved summer vegetable in Chinese cooking.
asianUses: Luffa with egg stir-fry (丝瓜炒蛋)
